symptoms: Uniform seed emergence
Robust taproot development
Main stems completely free from dark lesions, cracking, or vascular discoloration
Expansive, deep green, and unblemished foliage
High square (flower bud) and boll retention without signs of premature shedding, necrosis, or bacterial rot
prevention: Ensure soil temperature at planting depth (4 inches) exceeds 18 C (65 F) to prevent damping-off fungi
Delint cotton seeds with concentrated sulphuric acid (H2SO4) to remove surface-borne pathogens
Early thinning of the plant stand to ensure adequate airflow
Early earthing up combined with potash application to strengthen the stem and optimize vascular health
Ensure crop rotation with non-host crops like sorghum or maize
monitoringAdvice: Ensure crop rotation is planned and executed
farmerFriendlyExplanation: A healthy cotton field has seedlings that come up evenly, deep green leaves without any spots, strong clean stems, and keeps its flower buds and bolls without dropping them. In local terminology, a healthy cotton crop is referred to as స్వస్థ పత్తి (Swastha pathi) in Telugu and स्वस्थ कपास (Swasth kapas) in Hindi.

symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on the cotyledons that turn brown (Seedling Blight)
Girdling of the hypocotyl, potentially killing the young seedling
Scattered, small, dark-green, water-soaked spots on the lower leaf surface (Angular Leaf Spot)
Highly angular brown to black spots on leaves (constrained by veins)
Vein Necrosis (veins turning completely black)
Dark brown to black elongated necrotic lesions on the main stem and petioles (Black Arm)
Deep structural cracks, gummosis (oozing), and girdling of the stem
Stem becomes highly brittle and snaps easily under wind pressure
Water-soaked, sunken spots on bolls (Boll Rot)
Premature bursting of bolls
Bright yellow bacterial ooze staining developing lint
Destruction of seed viability
earlySymptoms: Water-soaked lesions on the cotyledons that turn brown
Scattered, small, dark-green, water-soaked spots on the lower leaf surface (Angular Leaf Spot)
advancedSymptoms: Vein Necrosis, with leaf veins turning completely black
Dark brown to black elongated necrotic lesions (Black Arm) on stems/petioles, causing cracking, gummosis, and stem girdling
Sunken spots on bolls (Boll Rot) causing premature bursting and yellow staining of lint
causes: Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. malvacearum (gram-negative, motile bacterium)
Pathogen persistence in dried plant debris in the soil

spreadConditions.rainfall: Heavy rain splashed by strong winds

low: Ensure seeds are not saved from an infected field
medium: Apply recommended prophylactic antibiotic/copper sprays if angular spots appear on leaves
high: Curative chemical treatment (foliar spray of Streptomycin + Copper oxychloride) to prevent stem invasion

organicTreatments: Deep plow to destroy infected plant debris

chemicalTreatments.notes: Curative (Early) chemical spray to stop bacteria from entering stems.

prevention: Strict seed sanitation and seed treatment
Delint seeds with concentrated sulphuric acid
Rogue out volunteer plants and deep plow
monitoringAdvice: Monitor seedling cotyledons for water-soaked brown lesions
Monitor lower leaf surfaces for angular, dark-green water-soaked spots
farmerFriendlyExplanation: A highly aggressive bacterial infection that creates sharp, square-shaped black spots on the leaves. It rapidly moves into the main stem, turning it black and brittle, causing branches to break off and the cotton bolls to rot before they open. The farmer must never save seeds from infected fields and must spray antibiotics mixed with copper at the first sign of spots. Locally known as కాలా బజూ రోగ్ / కోణీయ పత్తీ ధబ్బా (Kala baju rog / Koniya patti dhabba) in Hindi and బ్యాక్టీరియా ఆకుమచ్చ / నల్లమచ్చ తెగులు (Bacteria aakumacha / Nallamacha tegulu) in Telugu.

symptoms: Upward or downward curling of the leaf margins
Abnormal thickening and swelling of the leaf veins on the underside of the leaves
Unique cup-shaped enations (abnormal leaf-like outgrowths) developing directly from thickened veins
Shrunk internodes leading to severe stunting of the plant
Dramatically reduced or entirely halted square and boll formation
earlySymptoms: Distinctive upward or downward curling of the leaf margins
Thickening and swelling of the leaf veins on the underside of the leaves
advancedSymptoms: Unique cup-shaped enations on the veins on the underside of the leaves
Shrunk internodes causing severe stunting of the plant and a bushy appearance
Complete cessation of square and boll formation
causes: Transmission exclusively by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci)
Reservoirs in alternate weed hosts like Abutilon indicum and Solanum nigrum

low: Deploy yellow sticky traps (1 foot above canopy)
medium: Foliar spray of Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) 5% combined with Neem oil at 5 ml/L of water at the first sign of vector
high: Immediate uprooting and burning of virally infected plants to protect the rest of the field
Chemical spray (Diafenthiuron 50% WP or Flonicamid 50% WG) when pest population reaches ETL

organicTreatments: Eradicate alternate weed hosts like Abutilon indicum
Deploy yellow sticky traps at 1 foot above canopy
Foliar spray of Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) 5% combined with Neem oil at 5 ml/L of water

chemicalTreatments.sprayInterval: Spray when whitefly population reaches ETL (5 to 10 nymphs or adults per leaf)
Spray when whitefly population reaches ETL (5 to 10 nymphs or adults per leaf)

prevention: Eradicate alternate weed hosts (Abutilon indicum and Solanum nigrum) near the cotton fields
Deploy yellow sticky traps above the canopy
Integrated vector control to keep whitefly populations below ETL
monitoringAdvice: Check underside of the leaves for whitefly vector presence and vein thickening
Monitor ETL: spray when whitefly population reaches 5 to 10 nymphs or adults per leaf
farmerFriendlyExplanation: An incurable virus carried by tiny white flies. When they bite the plant, the virus enters the sap, causing leaves to curl up, veins underneath to swell, and the plant to stop growing and producing cotton. Farmers must immediately pull out and burn any curled plants, clear weeds, and spray neem oil or insecticides to kill the whiteflies. Known as పత్తీ మోరోడ్ వైరస్ (Patti morod virus) in Hindi and ఆకు ముడత వైరస్ (Aaku mudatha virus) in Telugu.

symptoms: General loss of turgor
Noticeable wilt during the heat of the day (even with adequate soil moisture)
Yellowing (chlorosis) starting at margins of lower leaves and moving inward
Leaf tissue necrosis
Continuous, dark brown discoloration of vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) inside the stem/taproot
Rapid death of seedlings (mimicking damping-off)
earlySymptoms: Wilt during the heat of the day
Yellowing (chlorosis) starting at the margins of lower leaves
advancedSymptoms: Continuous, dark brown discoloration of vascular tissues inside the lower stem or upper taproot when cut longitudinally
Complete defoliation and death of the plant
causes: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum (soil-borne fungal pathogen)
Pathogen survival as chlamydospores in the soil
Root penetration aided by plant-parasitic root-knot nematodes

spreadConditions.season: Monocropping of cotton, poor drainage, acidic soils

low: Uproot and burn the dead plants to reduce soil contamination
medium: Perform longitudinal cut of a wilting plant stem to confirm dark brown vascular staining
high: Do not plant cotton in that specific patch the following year without heavy soil treatment

organicTreatments: Seed treatment prior to sowing with Trichoderma viride @ 4g/kg or Bacillus subtilis @ 10g/kg
Fortify soil by applying Trichoderma viride @ 1.0 kg/acre mixed thoroughly with 20 kg FYM as a basal application
Rotate cotton with non-host cereal crops
prevention: Preventative biological seed treatments (Trichoderma viride or Bacillus subtilis)
Rigorous crop rotation with non-host cereals
monitoringAdvice: Monitor plants for wilting during the heat of the day
Perform destructive check (cut stem longitudinally) to inspect for dark brown vascular staining in wilting plants
farmerFriendlyExplanation: A soil fungus that invades the plant's roots and clogs its water pipes (veins). Since the plant cannot drink water, it droops and turns yellow from the bottom up, eventually dying. To confirm, cut the stem of a wilting plant; if the inside is stained dark brown, it is Fusarium wilt. Uproot and burn dead plants, rotate crops, and treat soil/seeds with bio-fungicides like Trichoderma. Locally known as ఉకట రోగ్ (Ukata rog) in Hindi and వడలు తెగులు (Vadalu tegulu) in Telugu.
